extracted.intended_audience: Founders/legislators and educators designing the education and cultural censorship for guardians in an ideal state (readers of Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidelines for selecting, composing, and censoring stories, poetry, and pedagogical content for the youth (especially future guardians) so as to form virtuous, courageous, temperate citizens. Includes moral-psychological standards for character, rules for depiction of gods and heroes, and stylistic distinctions in narrative form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleness to friends and fierceness to enemies (guardian character)
rubrics_metrics.description: A guardian must be gentle to his familiars and acquaintances and the reverse to strangers; the combination of gentleness and spiritedness is required in a good guardian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a guardian lacks either gentleness toward friends or fierceness toward enemies he will not be fit; the dog is offered as a model: well-bred dogs welcome acquaintances and are hostile to strangers. The trait implies both a loving/knowing orientation toward friends and spirited protectiveness toward foes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophic love of learning as part of guardian nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Those likely to be gentle to friends and fierce to enemies must by nature be lovers of wisdom and knowledge (philosophers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The love of learning is equated with philosophy: guardians should unite philosophy with spirit, swiftness and strength. The implication is that character formation must cultivate intellectual discernment as well as courage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education sequence: music (literature) before gymnastics
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional twofold education—music (including literature) and gymnastic—is to be ordered with music/literature taught first, because early stories shape the forming character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The beginning is the most important part of any work for young and tender minds; tales given in early childhood leave indelible impressions and therefore must be carefully chosen before physical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish censorship of fictional tales; authorize only approved stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders must establish a censorship of writers of fiction: censors should accept good tales and reject bad ones, and mothers and nurses should tell only authorized stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let poets and reciters be constrained to compose in approved forms; many existing tales must be discarded. The aim: fashion the mind of youth with authorised tales even more carefully than the body is moulded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit false or blameworthy representations of gods and heroes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tales that make erroneous representations of the nature of gods and heroes (bad lies) must be rejected—for example, the Hesiodic account of Uranus and Cronus is called a ‘bad lie’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such stories are necessary at all, they should only be told to a very few in mysterious rites with unusual sacrifices; otherwise they should be buried in silence. Rationale: such tales can justify crimes and vices by precedent or divine example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid recounting quarrels/strife among gods and heroic immorality
rubrics_metrics.description: Narratives of wars in heaven, plots and fightings of the gods, and quarrels of gods and heroes with relatives must not be admitted into the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young persons cannot judge allegory from literal truth; such tales risk making quarrelling appear acceptable and so should be suppressed, neither embroidered on garments nor taught to children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of the divine: gods must be represented as good and not authors of evil
rubrics_metrics.description: God is always to be represented as truly good; since the good is not a cause of evil, poets must not make gods the authors of evil or suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject lines that depict Zeus or the gods as dispensers of both good and evil; poets must either avoid attributing evil to gods or explain misfortunes as just punishment that benefits the punished. Treat as a law for poets and reciters: god is cause of good only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit depicting gods as shape-shifters, deceivers, or liars
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow poets to present gods as magicians who change forms, disguise themselves, or deceive mankind (e.g., Proteus/Thetis disguises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the best and fairest things change least, gods—being perfect—do not change; representations of gods changing shape or deceiving should be disallowed as they make children fearful and impious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict lying: rulers may lie for public good; others must not lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Lying in words is sometimes useful (a ‘medicine’) but the privilege of lying should be reserved to rulers for the public good; private individuals who lie should be punished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: just as patients should tell physicians the truth, citizens must tell rulers truth; only rulers may employ deceit strategically (with enemies or citizens) for the State. Introducing lying as common practice is subversive and destructive to the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control depictions of the afterlife to prevent fear of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets must be asked to obliterate passages that depict the world below as horrible or terrifying—remove vivid imagery and names (Cocytus, Styx, ghosts, sapless shades).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians should fear slavery more than death; strong poetic charm of horrific passages makes them especially unsuitable for youth because they may render guardians too excitable or effeminate. Remove passages that depict souls as mindless or pitiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude lamentations and excessive mourning from guardians' exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Weepings and wailings of famous men should be removed from the education of guardians; the good man will bear loss with equanimity and need not lament as others do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reassign lamentation to women or baser men in stories so that guardians scorn such behavior. Avoid depictions (e.g., Priam’s rolling in the dirt) that model excessive sorrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid representations of persons of worth as overcome by laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must not be represented as given to laughter; excessive laughter produces violent reaction and unmanly excitement and must not be shown even of the gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disallow poetic passages that depict inextinguishable laughter among the gods (e.g., at Hephaestus) or that model uncontrolled mirth for citizens being educated to be serious defenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate temperance: obedience and self-control in youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance in youth consists chiefly in obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures; stories must promote these elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approve lines that show troops silent in awe of leaders and rebuke verses that glorify drunkenness, luxury, or complaining. Avoid modeling appetite-driven behavior as glorious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit stories that praise gifts, bribery, or love of money
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sing of ‘gifts persuading gods’ or otherwise encourage reception of gifts or loving money; tales that show heroes acting out of greed or accepting bribes should be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject counsel like Phoenix’s advising Achilles to accept gifts; avoid praising monetary motives or depicting reward as moral justification for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban depictions of heroes committing vile or impious acts (rape, insolence, sacrilege)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should not represent heroes or sons of gods committing horrid rapes, insolence to deities, sacrilege or similar impious acts; if told, poets must disclaim that such acts were done by them or that they were not divine offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either the poets must assert the acts did not occur, or deny the hero’s divine parentage; the goal is to prevent young people from excusing their vices by divine precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent moral laxity by denying that injustice is profitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets who claim that wicked men are often happy and the just miserable (that injustice is profitable when undetected) are to be forbidden; instead poets must present the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question of how to depict men depends on the prior inquiry into the nature and benefits of justice; until justice is shown to be advantageous, poets must be steered away from narratives that naturalize injustice as profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative style guidance: distinguish narration vs imitation (persona)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration may be simple (poet speaking in his own person), wholly imitative (poet speaking as another person), or a union of both (epic). The poet’s choice determines the mode of presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homer sometimes speaks as himself and sometimes takes the person of a character (Chryses). If the poet always remains himself it is simple narration; if he always assumes others it is imitation (as in tragedy). Epic combines both forms. The choice affects how readers hear and internalize the moral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make first tales models of virtuous thoughts for youth (truth and moral exemplarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tales which the young first hear should be models of virtuous thoughts; anything received at that age is likely to become indelible and unalterable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore the founders must know the general forms and limits poets must observe; while founders need not compose the tales, they must set rules so that early storytelling fosters virtue rather than vice.
